questions.q: Why is a view a better fit here than a materialized table that gets refreshed on a schedule?
options: A view has no stored data of its own and re-runs its query on every read, so it's always current with zero refresh logic to maintain
Views run faster than tables in every case
Tables cannot be queried by Power BI
Views automatically load new CSV files without a COPY INTO statement
questions.explain: For a project this small, a view's simplicity — always current, no refresh job to maintain — wins over the added complexity of a materialized table.

questions.q: What does CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW let you do that plain CREATE VIEW doesn't?
options: Update the view's definition in place later without dropping it first or re-pointing anything that already queries it
Grant privileges automatically to every role in the account
Load data directly into the view
Skip the WHERE clause entirely
questions.explain: CREATE OR REPLACE means a later tweak to the query just updates the view in place, which is friendlier to anything already depending on it.

questions.q: Why did the GRANT SELECT on the view have to wait until this lesson, rather than happening back in Lesson 6?
options: The view didn't exist yet in Lesson 6 — you can't grant access to an object before it's created
GRANT statements can only run on Mondays
Lesson 6 only covers warehouses, never views
SELECT grants require the view to already contain at least one row
questions.explain: Lesson 6 finished every grant that didn't depend on the view existing; this lesson creates the view and finishes the chain with the one grant that needed it.

questions.q: What's the real test that DRIFTWOOD_SUPPORT_ANALYST's access is set up correctly?
options: Switching into that role with USE ROLE and confirming the view actually returns rows, not just that the GRANT statements ran without errors
Checking that the role's name is spelled correctly
Confirming the warehouse is running
Re-running CREATE ROLE a second time
questions.explain: A GRANT running without an error doesn't prove the chain is complete — actually switching to the role and querying is the real proof.

questions.q: If you switch into DRIFTWOOD_SUPPORT_ANALYST and try to query RAW_TICKETS directly, what should happen?
options: It should fail — the role was never granted SELECT on the raw table, only on the summary view
It should succeed, since the role can see everything in the SUPPORT schema
It should succeed only on weekdays
It should automatically redirect to the view instead
questions.explain: Confirming the raw table query fails is proof the least-privilege design from Lesson 6 actually holds, not just that the view query works.
